A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the multinomial probot model is a good approximation of choice behavior for small m, but becomes a poor approximation as m increases.
the multinomial probot model of Myatt & Wallace (2003)[5] is a special case of our model, and the rates of decay in our model are different from those in their model.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the multinomial probot model is not well-suited to describing choice in environments with a large number of actions, as it predicts that the probability of choosing any particular action decays exponentially fast as the number of actions grows.

the rate of decay depends not only on the difference between the payoff of the optimal action and the payoff of the suboptimal action, but also on the difference between these two payoffs relative to the standard deviation of the shocks.

the multinomial probot model can be interpreted as a special case of a more general model of choice in which the payoﬀs to each of the n actions are subjected not to the average of a single shock, but to the average of n independent shocks.
